pulls.title: Testnet 5 (BIP95)
pulls.body:
Implements [BIP 95](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0095.md) (Testnet 5). Relative to Testnet 4 it removes the 20-minute minimum-difficulty exception, raises the minimum difficulty, and enforces [BIP 54](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0054.md) from block 1. The Genesis block has not been mined yet.

Based on #35793, only the top five commits belong to this PR.

Per the [discussion in a recent IRC meeting](https://bitcoin-irc.chaincode.com/bitcoin-core-dev/2026-07-30#1242502;): since BIP 95 activates BIP 54 from block 1, this depends on #35793 and won't make the v32 feature freeze. So we can review and settle the changes now, but leave this in draft until #35793 lands. Once reviewers are happy with the state of the draft here we can add the Genesis block and the network can get started without being included in a release. We can then ship a patched v32 release with Testnet 5 included. A solo-mining ckpool endpoint is likely being set up and will be advertised here. There are no DNS or fixed seeds yet.

pulls.title: txorphanage: bound orphan memory by storing transactions serialized
pulls.body:
The orphanage limits the "usage" of the orphans it stores, per peer and globally, to bound the amount of memory an attacker can make us hold on to. It uses weight as a proxy for that memory, on the assumption that weight is "often higher than the actual memory usage of the transaction".

That assumption does not hold for a deserialized transaction. Every witness stack element is an individually heap-allocated vector, costing its 24-byte slot in the stack vector plus a 32-byte minimum allocation, while only weighing 2WU. A transaction of 199,000 1-byte witness elements weighs 398,247WU (i.e. it is of standard weight, and witness standardness cannot be checked while the inputs are missing), but uses 11.1MB of memory: 28 times what is accounted for it, and one such orphan can be retained per peer.

Rather than change the accounting metric, keep orphans in serialized form, deserializing them again on the paths that hand them back out. Serialized, a transaction's memory usage is bounded by its weight, so the existing weight-based accounting becomes a true upper bound on memory and the worst case is the peers' combined allowances.

Admission, eviction and accounting behavior are unchanged: no transaction that was previously accepted is refused, so orphan resolution (and thus 1p1c package relay) keeps working for standard-weight transactions whose witnesses consist of many small elements, such as BitVM-style transactions.

pulls.title: [wip,nomerge,rfc] build: Require C++23 compiler
pulls.body:
C++23 for Bitcoin Core is mostly a "style update" on top of C++20. However, the workarounds to avoid C++23 keep accumulating and some parts of the code already use C++23 features, such as lambda attributes (https://github.com/bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess/commit/bdd0cd69418d189f62699d274a751cbf6d36bb43).

I don't know when it is fine to switch, but at some point, I think it is fine to require a C++23 compiler, so that [new stuff](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/34979#issuecomment-4448399166) is unlocked. Of course this requires bumping the minimum required compiler versions:

* GCC: 13
* Clang: 19

There are some C++23 features that aren't implemented (such as `<stacktrace>` not really shipped in any vanilla stdlib today), or e.g. `ranges::starts_with` not implemented until libstdc++-16. But overall I think we are better off using C++23 without those few features instead of waiting longer?

pulls.title: refactor : Reorder CBlockIndex members to save 8 bytes
pulls.body:
It seems we can save 8 bytes per CBlockIndex instance by reordering one class member. Moving one 8-byte field seems to avoid losing 2x 4 bytes to structure padding on a 64-bit build (on a 32-bit build, there is no gain).

I could not exactly measure the runtime gain from just this (smaller than RAM usage variation between 2 launches), but I confirmed there was about as many instances of CBlockIndex as blocks in the chain (increasing CBlockIndex size by 320 bytes increases RAM usage by ~300MB), so saving 8 bytes per instance should save about 8MB of RAM at current block height.

The gain is small, but it seems like it has no cost/risk, since that structure is not used for serialization, and just reordering here should have no side effects.

I saw a few other types that could gain a few bytes in size by doing something similar (for example, CTxIn), but they have far fewer instances in memory to make the change worth it.

pulls.title: rpc: handle malformed jsonrpc 2.0 requests correctly
pulls.body:
While reviewing #36642 I found something else we missed in JSON-RPC 2.0:

If we receive a malformed request we would assume that we couldn't parse it's jsonrpc version and send an HTTP error.  This is how the legacy jsonrpc server worked (despite that behavior not ever being part of any ratified jsonrpc spec) and we maintain it as Bitcoin "legacy" jsonrpc protocol. However it's possible to form a request that does properly indicate jsonrpc 2.0 but is still malformed. In that case, we should not send an HTTP error: the correct protocol is to respond with `HTTP 200 OK` and include the jsonrpc error message in the response.

The solution is to catch parse errors and then check if we know the request's jsonrpc version before responding.

We already correctly handle such malformed requests in batches and this is already tested in `test_batch_requests()` in `interface_rpc.py`

On master, the functional test in this PR actually crashes the node because the assumption is codified. Note that this crash requires:
1. RPC Authentication
2. A debug build

So this is not an urgent security fix, but a bug that might disrupt testing.

```
node0 stderr httprpc.cpp:46
    UniValue JSONErrorReply(UniValue, const JSONRPCRequest &, HTTPStatusCode &):
        'jreq.m_json_version != JSONRPCVersion::V2' check failed.
```


In release builds the node doesn't crash, but it returns HTTP 400 with a JSON-RPC 2.0 error body instead of HTTP 200.

pulls.title: http: update m_keep_alive under m_send_mutex
pulls.body:
`HTTPRemoteClient::Send()` sets `m_keep_alive` before taking `m_send_mutex` and appending the response to the send buffer, while the I/O thread reads it under `m_send_mutex` in `MaybeSendBytesFromBuffer()` right after the buffer drains to empty. The two updates are therefore not ordered with respect to each other, and a pipelining client can lose a response:

1. Response 1 (keep-alive) is partially sent and the I/O thread is still draining it.
2. Request 2 (`Connection: close`) is parsed from the receive buffer and dispatched to a worker (the send throttle from #36174 only holds a request back once the buffer exceeds `MAX_BODY_SIZE`).
3. The worker clears `m_keep_alive`; the I/O thread then finishes sending response 1, sees an empty buffer with `m_keep_alive == false`, and sets `m_disconnect`.
4. The worker appends response 2, which is dropped when the client is disconnected on the next loop iteration.

This PR moves the assignment into the critical section that appends the response, and turns the field from `std::atomic_bool` into a plain `bool GUARDED_BY(m_send_mutex)` so Clang's thread-safety analysis enforces the ordering (the only reader already holds the mutex). With the flag and the buffer updated together, the I/O thread can no longer observe "empty && !keep_alive" between two pipelined responses.

The ordering dates back to the initial HTTP server implementation (#35182); #35829/#36007 only moved the code. The window is small and `bitcoin-cli` does not pipeline, so this is a low-severity fix.

### Test

`http_pipelined_keepalive_close_tests` reproduces the interleaving deterministically with a mock socket: `Send()` fails with EAGAIN until the second request has been dispatched, then the I/O thread's next `Send()` (made while holding `m_send_mutex`) signals the worker to write its reply, waits for it to reach `HTTPRemoteClient::Send()`, and only then flushes the first reply. Sends are refused again until the test releases them, so the second reply is only delivered if the I/O loop kept the connection open. Without the first commit the test fails with `server.GetConnectionsCount() == 1 has failed [0 != 1]`: the client was disconnected with the second reply still in its send buffer.

pulls.title: mempool: recalculate stale BIP68 lockpoints in removeForReorg
pulls.body:
When a reorg lowers the tip, `removeForReorg` can evict BIP68 transactions that are still valid at the new tip, together with all their descendants.

A transaction that spends an unconfirmed parent gets its lockpoints cached with that input at height tip+1. After `invalidateblock`, `TestLockPointValidity` can still pass on those cached lockpoints (always when every input was unconfirmed, since `maxInputBlock` is then genesis; and with mixed confirmed and unconfirmed inputs when the confirmed input's block survives), so `CheckSequenceLocksAtTip` is evaluated against stale values and the transaction is removed.

The fix, suggested by ismaelsadeeq, is to never evict on cached lockpoints alone: if they are not valid at the new tip, or the cached sequence-lock check fails, recalculate them with `CalculateLockPointsAtTip` and evict only if the fresh result also fails. This covers height-based and time-based locks alike, at the cost of some recalculations that turn out to be unnecessary.

test_reorg_stale_lockpoints() in feature_bip68_sequence.py covers four cases across a reorg: a BIP68-disabled child, a BIP68-enabled child of an unconfirmed parent, a child with mixed confirmed and unconfirmed inputs, and a time-based zero lock where the reorg lowers the median time past (test by Bicaru20). The test fails on master, and the mixed-input case also fails on the earlier genesis-only version of this fix.

Reproducer for unpatched nodes:
https://gist.github.com/javierpmateos/c55d365973adbf488a852dc5e0b77dec

Same class of issue fixed for TRUC in #33504.

Closes #35007

pulls.title: orphanage: Fix orphan reconsideration disconnect hole, add 1p1c invariant harness
pulls.body:
The first commit adds `p2p_1p1c_liveness`, an end-to-end fuzz target for parent and child relay. It
  drives a real PeerManager with real messages and validation, and checks that if an honest peer announces
  the child of an acceptable parent and child, the child reaches the mempool within a bounded time,
  whatever other peers do. Known liveness holes are marked in the target as flags that turn the check off
  once opened, including this one. With that flag turned off, the target finds this bug on master from an
  empty corpus in under an hour on one core; an earlier version found it first
  (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36371#issuecomment-5937814761).

  The second commit hands reconsideration over to a remaining announcer when the marked announcement is
  erased, and removes the flag.

Follow-up PR to fill the holes is here: https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36506

pulls.title: test: SRD tie-break test
pulls.body:
Pr #33223  adjusts the weight selection to keep the lighter coin when two coins have the same value, but the test has two mistakes

1. It builds `mixed_weight_pool` but passes `utxo_pool` to `TestSRDSuccess`.
2. There is nothing enforcing coin eviction because the current max weight (`4 * 3 * 67` = 804 WU) fits any two coins (544 WU)

The old existing test does not check the fix:
If you reverse #33223, it still passes 20/20 tests, which means it misses the tie-break
Other coin selection tests like `spend_tests`, `wallet_send.py`, `wallet_fundrawtransaction.py` do not catch the broken tie-break
The fix
The PR uses `mixed_weight_pool` instead of `utxo_pool`.
The PR adds an extra light coin so that only two light coins can fit together and evicts a coin on every tie to pass.
It also lowers the max weight to `4 * 2 * (P2WPKH_INPUT_VSIZE - 1)` = 536 WU; SRD now has to evict the heavier coin on every tie to succeed
Adds a second (67 vB) light coin to the pool
This should show 20/20 failed tests with [bitcoin#33223](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/33223) reverted and 20/20 passing without the revert
Steps to reproduce:
Revert the #33223  change in `src/wallet/coinselection.cpp`

```
git show eff9e798b9 -- src/wallet/coinselection.cpp | git apply -R
```

Build and run the tests

```
cmake --build build --target test_bitcoin
build/bin/test_bitcoin --run_test=coinselection_tests/srd_test
```

Expected results: After the revert, it should fail on this PR and pass on master

pulls.title: net: require a dedicated bind for automatic Tor
pulls.body:
**Problem:** When the automatic onion service has no dedicated `-bind=<addr>=onion`, Tor forwards incoming connections to the first normal P2P bind. A wildcard onion bind also fails to identify incoming Tor connections. In either case, network classification is incorrect and Tor peers may inherit permissions granted to the Tor daemon's IP address.

**Fix:** Refuse startup when `-listenonion` is enabled and an explicit `-bind` configuration lacks a dedicated, non-wildcard onion bind or includes a wildcard onion bind, following [the recommendation in #34892](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34892#issuecomment-5541662236). Users should add a specific `-bind=<addr>=onion` or set `-listenonion=0`.

Because `-listenonion` is enabled by default when listening, existing configurations with only a normal `-bind` must also be updated. Nodes without explicit `-bind` options retain the default dedicated onion listener.

pulls.title: rpc: reset id and version per batch element
pulls.body:
In a JSON-RPC batch, an element that is not an object gets an error reply with the id and version of the element before it.

`ExecuteHTTPRPC` uses one request object for the whole batch. `parse()` throws on a non-object before it resets `id` and `m_json_version`. For `[{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"getblockcount","id":"X"}, 2]` the reply has two objects with `"id":"X"`, one with a result and one with an error. If the first element is a notification, the error is dropped. I reset both fields at the top of `parse()`, so the error is the one the first element of a batch already gets. The new case in `interface_rpc.py` fails on master and passes with this change.

pulls.title: interfaces: Avoid node crashes from invalid Chain IPC calls
pulls.body:
**Problem:** A program using the `Chain` IPC interface from #29409 can crash `bitcoin-node` with a single bad call: asking for a block hash above the tip, leaving the transaction argument of `broadcastTransaction` or `checkChainLimits` unset, or returning an error from a notification handler. Separately, `findAncestorByHash` reports success when the descendant block is unknown (#36472). The `Chain` methods were written for in-process C++ callers like the wallet, which follow documented preconditions, so they assert or dereference null instead of returning errors.

**Solution:** Make these `Chain` methods in `src/node/interfaces.cpp` return errors for invalid arguments, catch and log IPC errors from notification handlers, and fix the `findAncestorByHash` check. Three small commits, each with unit tests in `src/test/interfaces_tests.cpp`. Valid calls behave the same as before. Details are in the commit messages.

This PR does not depend on #29409, but the fixes matter if it is merged and `interfaces::Chain` is exposed over IPC. The problems were reported by zaidmstrr, willcl-ark and xyzconstant while reviewing #29409, and by enirox001 in #36472. The `findAncestorByHash` fix is the same one previously proposed by Romansage6 and Yudis-bit in #36473, #36484 and #36490.

pulls.title: http: disconnect clients that never finish a request
pulls.body:
The -rpcservertimeout timer only measures inactivity. Every read from a client resets it, so a client that keeps sending bytes without ever completing a request can hold the connection for ever. 

Connection slots are capped by default 16 or by -rpcmaxconnections. Once those slots are taken, the server stops accepting new connections. Because no request ever completes the authentication functions are never hit. 
The impact is low because RPC port binds to localhost by default, so this is a robustness fix rather than a remotely exploitable security issue.

<details> <summary> How to reproduce </summary>

To reproduce: start a node with -rpcmaxconnections=2, open two sockets, and write "GET / HTTP/1.1\r\n" one byte at a time with ten seconds between bytes. bitcoin-cli getblockcount then hangs until one of the (trickling) sockets is closed.

</details>

The fix adds a second deadline next to the idle timer. It is armed on the first byte of a request and expires after -rpcservertimeout (the same value as the idle timer). This timer also does not resets or is extended by later reads. Completing request parsing clears the deadline, so a long-running RPC keeps its connection as before. The deadline is deferred while a worker holds the request, for the same reason the idle timer is. It is restarted while response bytes
are written, because the client cannot start a new request during that window. -rpcservertimeout=0 disables both timers. No new option is added.

Disclaimer this bug is found by utilizing ASTRA. Verified using KIMI 3 and Claude.

pulls.title: fuzz: add a custom mutator for PSBT
pulls.body:
The `partially_signed_transaction_deserialize` target feeds raw bytes to the PSBT parser. Byte-level mutations rarely produce well-formed key-value maps with valid keydata (pubkeys, xpubs, control blocks, DER signatures, etc), so most inputs are rejected early and the deeper per-field parsing is rarely reached.

This PR adds a custom mutator for PSBT which is ported from bitcoinfuzz (with some changes).  The mutator splits the input into global/input/output maps of key-value records, applies the mutations and serializes the result again. The first commit is a preparation to allow targets to provide a custom mutator by adding an optional `mutator` field to
`FuzzTargetOptions`. 

note: LLM assisted on porting the custom mutator.

pulls.title: Silent Payments:  Sending (take 2)
pulls.body:
This PR is part of integrating silent payments into Bitcoin Core. It is the second iteration of https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/28201. Status and tracking for the project is managed in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/28536

Prerequisite PRs:
- [x] https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35301

### Sending

**Silent Payments logic**
Key things to note in this PR:

pulls.title: rpc: Report -rpcwhitelist denials as JSON-RPC errors
pulls.body:
This PR adds two JSON-RPC error codes for requests refused by `-rpcwhitelist`, which until now got an HTTP 403 status with an empty body:

- `RPC_METHOD_NOT_PERMITTED` (-38) is returned for a refused request, with HTTP 200 for JSON-RPC 2.0 requests and 403 for legacy 1.x requests.
- `RPC_REQUEST_NOT_EXECUTED` (-39) is returned for the other requests in a refused batch. A refused batch now gets HTTP 200 and an array with an error for each request, and still runs none of them.

**Problem:** `-rpcwhitelist` errors are currently handled differently from other JSON-RPC errors, so clients report them with vague or misleading messages, and for JSON-RPC 2.0 requests the handling does not follow [documented behavior](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/master/doc/JSON-RPC-interface.md#json-rpc-11-vs-20). Specifically, requests refused by `-rpcwhitelist` get HTTP 403 with an empty body, so the refusal shows up as a generic transport error rather than a specific JSON-RPC error. This is especially a problem for JSON-RPC 2.0 requests, which are [supposed to](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/commit/bf1a1f1662427fbf1a43bb951364eface469bdb7) report failed method calls only as JSON-RPC errors, not HTTP errors. The empty reply causes a concrete problem when JSON-RPC requests are sent over IPC instead of HTTP: `bitcoin-cli -ipcconnect` receives only the response body, so a refused call prints a JSON type error instead of a permission error, as described in a [private security review](https://ipcbugs.ofsky.org/audits/ar-56/). Over HTTP, `bitcoin-cli` currently stops at the 403 status and prints only "server returned HTTP error 403" instead of the actual error.

**Solution:** Report whitelist denials like any other failed call: a JSON-RPC error in the body, with the HTTP status the request's version calls for. This brings the behavior in line with the documentation. `bitcoin-cli` then prints the permission error over both HTTP and IPC, with no change to the IPC interface. Small change to `src/httprpc.cpp` and `src/rpc/protocol.h`, with tests in `rpc_whitelist.py` and `interface_ipc_cli.py`. Details in the commit messages.

Compatibility: HTTP clients that send `"jsonrpc": "2.0"` or batches and check for a 403 status need to read the error code instead. Single 1.x requests keep the 403 status, now with an error body.

Open question for review: `RPC_METHOD_NOT_PERMITTED` could be named `RPC_ACCESS_DENIED`, and `RPC_REQUEST_NOT_EXECUTED` is documented as batch-specific but would fit any request refused before it runs.

pulls.title: mempool: remove time-based transaction expiry
pulls.body:
This is a simple mempool PR that fixes #33510.

Evicting mempool transactions by age (`-mempoolexpiry`, default two weeks) is
incentive-incompatible: it may drop transactions that could still be mined 
As discussed IRL and in #33510, this PR hence removes age-based eviction entirely.

Transactions now leave the mempool only via size limiting (`-maxmempool`),
replacement, conflicts, or inclusion in a block. The `EXPIRY` removal reason is
dropped. `-mempoolexpiry` is retained as a hidden no-op that warns when set, so
existing configurations keep starting.

Nice side effects:
- With expiry gone, the `entry_time` index has no readers. Removing it saves an
  ordered-tree node per mempool entry and drops a now unused Boost
  include.
- The `DynamicMemoryUsage()` per-entry estimate drops from three indexes to
  two, so within the same `-maxmempool` budget the mempool fits slightly more
  transactions.

pulls.title: script: store interpreter stack elements as reference-counted objects
pulls.body:
Modifies the script interpreter to represent stack elements internally using smart pointers, making duplication memory-cheap, and giving us caching keys which are cheap and guaranteed unique by the compiler. First part of a 2-part project to improve script interpreter performance in preparation for PQ signatures. 

No consensus changes - a pure performance improvement refactor.

## Motivation 

We presently have `MAX_SCRIPT_ELEMENT_SIZE = 520`, but in the near future, motivated by the need for PQ signature schemes, we may want to introduce soft fork changes which increase the max stack element size for new output types well into the multi-kilobyte range. This may be perhaps as high as 10kb or more given the current landscape of PQ signature schemes' sizes. 

Ongoing related work:

- https://github.com/SHRINCS/shrincs-bip/blob/main/leaf-version-0xC2.mediawiki#user-content-Relaxing_the_Max_Stack_Element_Size
- https://github.com/SHRINCS/shrincs-bip/pull/76

This poses a new problem to today's implementations if deployed naively. 

Today's Bitcoin script interpreter moves around raw mutable byte vectors to represent stack elements. When those elements are duplicated, the underlying byte vectors are deep-copied. When hash opcodes execute, they always invoke the corresponding hash function and fully ingest the top stack element. Duplication and hashing cost only a single weight unit in tapscript, with no upper limit on how many times they can be executed, aside from implicit limits due to the 10,000 byte script size maximum.

If we were to simply up the stack element size limit from 520b to 10kb, then we exacerbate an existing DoS vector on bitcoin nodes: Push a big (today 520b, maybe someday 10kb) stack element, then duplicate and hash it over and over. Worst case would be a script like this:

```cpp
<big_blob> DUP DUP [DUP3 RMD160 DROP RMD160 DROP RMD160 DROP]...
```  

...with the `[...]` part repeating up to the script size limit. RMD160 is used because it lacks hardware acceleration support and so performs significantly worse than even HASH256 or HASH160, making a more effective CPU attack.

This costs the attacker only \~20000 weight units (10kb for the script, 10kb for the stack element), but forces all validators to evaluate OP_RIPEMD160 about 4284 times, each on the same 10kb input. That's about 672588 RMD160 compressions in software.

I ran a benchmark (not in this PR) using this style of script with 520b and 10kb script elements. 

- 520b: validation takes about **3 milliseconds**
- 10,000b: validation takes about **52 milliseconds**

## This PR

(idea credit: EthanHeilman)

To address this risk, we would want to implement a **hash cache** for all the hashing opcodes. However, to implement such a cache safely in consensus, we need extremely robust cache keys. A collision in the cache key would be a consensus bug because the cache would return the wrong hash for a given input. But we can't cryptographically hash the inputs to compute a cache key... that is the same work we are trying to avoid with the cache. 

Instead we can kill two birds with two PRs. 

1. Replace stack elements with ref-counting pointers, so OP_DUP et al duplicate pointers and not the underlying raw bytes. :arrow_backward:  **THIS PR**
2. Implement a hash cache keyed by the stack element pointers. Each cache entry holds a handle to the key pointer so that the key doesn't get dropped and the pointer reallocated for a new stack element (which would cause a consensus bug). Cache key uniqueness is guaranteed by the compiler.  :arrow_backward: **Future PR**

Stage 1 reduces the asymmetric memory inflation attack allowed by OP_DUP et al. Stage 2 fixes the asymmetric CPU DoS attack. To be clear, neither stage fully prevents an attacker from uploading a series of large stack elements, and duplicating/hashing them. But we **do** force attackers to pay for those operations with fees and block space. 

I have both stage 1 and 2 implemented locally and can show benchmarks to prove the effect of the cache, if desired. I could have submitted it all as one PR but both stages are atomic and could do well with separate review.

pulls.title: validation: check the most recent AssumeUTXO commitment during IBD
pulls.body:
**Problem:** AssumeUTXO verifies imported UTXOs against a hash we bake into the binary.
Every node reconstructs the same UTXO set during ordinary IBD, but [does not check its hash against the existing AssumeUTXO commitment](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/32377).

**Fix:** During ordinary block validation, verify the AssumeUTXO hash when block connection reaches the corresponding block.
Log mismatches and raise a GUI/RPC warning while allowing IBD to continue.
Flush pending changes to disk before hashing the UTXO set and comparing the result with the commitment.

Keep only the latest AssumeUTXO commitment per network to limit the extra hashing work during IBD, and update the release process to replace it.
Users who need older snapshots for research or other purposes can use a compatible older release or restore the corresponding commitment as `m_assumeutxo_data` and recompile.

> There is currently nothing preventing us to receive TCP urgent data, which would never be returned by `recv()`. Linux's `poll()` is indifferent to this, but the `select()` socket monitoring may keep reporting it as pending on some platforms.

pulls.title: net: serve `MSG_BLOCK` by stripping witnesses in place
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Serving blocks to legacy nodes currently decodes and reserializes them just to remove witnesses. `MSG_WITNESS_BLOCK` already avoids this work by serving the stored bytes directly. Faster witnessless IBD, as proposed in [#36476](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/36476), also needs peers to serve these blocks efficiently.

**Fix:** Read disk-backed, non-Signet `MSG_BLOCK` replies into an owned byte buffer, check the header's proof of work and expected hash, and strip witness ranges from that buffer in place.

Extract a shared helper so decoding transactions and skipping their bytes follow the same encoding rules. Signet keeps `ReadBlock` for its solution check. Header checks now precede transaction parsing, so records corrupted in both places can log a different error.

**Performance:**

Time to read a block from disk and build its non-witness message:

| Block | Before | After | Speedup |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `block413567` | 1.31 ms | 0.147 ms | **8.9x** |
| Same block with synthetic witnesses | 3.47 ms | 0.374 ms | **9.3x** |

The synthetic fixture adds a 512-byte witness item and an empty item to every input.

**Related work:** This extends the raw witness-block serving added in [#13151](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/13151). The [#13011 discussion](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/13011#issuecomment-383145046) and the closed [#13098](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/13098) identify unnecessary transaction hashing when serving historical blocks. The implementation also builds on the bulk block reads introduced in [#31551](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/31551).

pulls.title: net, http: always set accepted sockets as non-blocking
pulls.body:
A mistake here would be critical, as it would allow a malicious peer to stall us indefinitely for free. This is not currently an issue because:
- while on Linux accepted sockets do not inherit O_NONBLOCK, we always send() and recv() on Linux/macOS/BSD with MSG_DONTWAIT;
- while on Windows MSG_DONTWAIT is unset, accepted sockets do inherit the non-blocking option [^1].

Therefore, set accepted sockets (inbound P2P connections and HTTP clients) as non-blocking explicitly, like CreateSockOS() does for the sockets it creates. A belt-and-suspenders check costs virtually nothing here, and we already have similar ones for less important options (such as TCP_NODELAY, which as far as i know is inherited by accepted sockets on all our supported platforms).

[^1]: Source is [this](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winsock2/nf-winsock2-accept#remarks) implicit remark in the accept() doc, plus my own testing.

pulls.title: ipc: Expose Chain interface to IPC clients
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Processes connected to `bitcoin-node` over IPC (with `-ipcbind`) can use the `Mining` interface, but they can't currently use the `Chain` interface read chain data or follow chain events. Chain data could be useful to third-party clients and Bitcoin Core's own wallet could use this as well to run in a separate process (#10102). But exposing all of `interfaces::Chain` to external clients would make its methods hard to change, since the wallet uses them as internal API (#34981).

**Solution:** Add capnp wrappers for `interfaces::Chain`, split into two interfaces backed by the same C++ class:

- `Chain`, returned by `Init.makeChain`, is stable. It follows Cap'n Proto schema evolution rules, so existing clients keep working as methods are added. It starts with the five block lookup methods: `findBlock`, `findFirstBlockWithTimeAndHeight`, `findAncestorByHeight`, `findAncestorByHash` and `findCommonAncestor`.
- `UnstableChain`, returned by `Init.makeUnstableChain`, extends `Chain` with every other method, for Bitcoin Core's own clients. It can change in any way between releases. Incompatible changes renumber `makeUnstableChain`, so old clients get an error instead of calling the wrong methods.

Methods can move from `UnstableChain` to `Chain` once we're willing to support them for external use. `test/functional/interface_ipc.py` shows a Python client calling both interfaces. Like the existing IPC interfaces, these are only available to processes that can connect to the IPC socket, which already grants full node access through `Init.makeRpc`.

**Merge order:** This depends on bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess#377 and bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess#379 and a subtree update that includes them (this PR currently carries that bump, plus a `-Wc++23-lambda-attributes` build fix that goes with it), and on #36520, which fixes node crashes IPC clients could trigger with invalid `Chain` arguments.

pulls.title: wallet: fill PSBT_GLOBAL_XPUB
pulls.body:
Closes #27583.

`PSBT_GLOBAL_XPUB` already serializes, deserializes and merges when PSBTs are combined. Nothing writes it, so a PSBT produced by the wallet never carries it, and a signer that only has the file cannot rebuild the multisig from it. Today Specter [fills the field itself](https://github.com/cryptoadvance/specter-desktop/blob/8843e2f0640a9adc129f9ab6afe5ecb9632e7c5b/src/cryptoadvance/specter/wallet/wallet.py#L1866-L1881) after getting the PSBT from Core.

<details><summary>Before and after with the BitBox02 and Trezor simulators</summary>

A 2-of-3 `wsh(sortedmulti(...))` on regtest with the simulator as one co-signer, signed through HWI 3.2.0. The "before" file is the same PSBT with its `PSBT_GLOBAL_XPUB` records removed, so nothing else differs.

| | without the field | with the field |
|---|---|---|
| BitBox02 | refuses, `This BitBox02 is not one of the cosigners` | signs |
| Trezor T | signs, co-signer nodes sent with zeroed chain codes and no derivation paths | signs, nodes sent with the real chain codes and paths |

What `parse_multisig` hands the Trezor for the change output:

```
without: global xpubs=0  zeroed chain codes=3/3  depths=[0, 0, 0]  paths=[[], [], []]
with   : global xpubs=3  zeroed chain codes=0/3  depths=[4, 4, 4]  paths=[[1, 0], [1, 0], [1, 0]]
```

</details>

A new `Descriptor` accessor returns the extended keys a descriptor is built from, and `DescriptorScriptPubKeyMan::FillPSBT` writes those of every descriptor with an input or an output in the PSBT. That covers `walletcreatefundedpsbt`, `walletprocesspsbt`, `send`, `sendall`, `psbtbumpfee` and the GUI send dialog, which all go through `CWallet::FillPSBT`.

Only the keys BIP 174 allows are added, the ones that derive, through unhardened steps alone, a key the PSBT gives a derivation path for. So a key expression ending in `/*h` adds nothing.

Whoever holds a PSBT from the wallet can now derive the addresses of the descriptors it uses. Setting `bip32derivs` to false in `walletcreatefundedpsbt` or `walletprocesspsbt` leaves the field out, along with the derivation paths.

`descriptorprocesspsbt` is left out, since it signs from the descriptors it is given without going through the wallet, and I intend to cover it as a follow-up.

pulls.title: contrib: fix dead null-byte check in linearize-data.py
pulls.body:
`linearize-data.py` hangs on any block file that ends in zero padding.

Reproduce:

```
mkdir -p /tmp/lin/blocks && cd /tmp/lin
python3 -c "open('blocks/blk00000.dat','wb').write(bytes(4096))"
printf '%064d\n' 0 > hashlist.txt
printf 'input=blocks\nhashlist=hashlist.txt\noutput_file=bootstrap.dat\ngenesis=%064d\n' 0 > linearize.cfg
python3 /path/to/bitcoin/contrib/linearize/linearize-data.py linearize.cfg
```

Before, it never returns:

```
Read 1 hashes
Input file blocks/blk00000.dat
<hangs>
```

After:

```
Read 1 hashes
Input file blocks/blk00000.dat
Input file blocks/blk00001.dat
Premature end of block data
```

Indexing a bytes object returns an int in Python 3, so `inhdr[0] == "\0"` is always false and the zero-padding check never fires. The script instead falls through to the magic-bytes search, which advances one byte per iteration; at the end of the file `read(8)` returns 7 bytes and `seek(-7)` moves back to the same offset, so it loops there forever and the `Premature end of block data` path is never reached.

Block files are preallocated in `BLOCKFILE_CHUNK_SIZE` (16 MiB) chunks and only truncated once finalized, so the most recent blk*.dat normally ends in padding.

This is reached whenever the hashlist references blocks that are not in the blocks directory. The most common case is a pruned datadir, which the script explicitly supports - `getFirstBlockFileId()` starts at the first surviving blk file for exactly that reason. The intended response is "Premature end of block data", but that path is never reached.

This is the same one-line change as #32978, which was closed because no reproduction was provided. Happy to add a test to `test/functional/feature_loadblock.py` instead if that is preferred.

pulls.title: [DONTMERGE] Test run with reproducer for forced chunked recv
pulls.body:
WARNING: NOT INTENDED FOR MERGING!

Performing a test run with forced chunked recv. 

All networking code using sockets must not make assumption about the chunking of the incoming/outgoing data, and should be resilient against any chunking. Normally, the chunking of the sends of the writer dictate the chunking of the receives at the reader, but this is not guaranteed by IP/TCP, intermediate networking elements may change the packet structure.

This branch contains a stress test reproducer. For every socket read, `recv()` is not called to read all available data, but data is read and returned in smaller chunks. The goal is to test code for robustness in face of unexpected chunking of the data.

This PR will be closed once the test runs complete, and kept for reference (some tests are expected to fail).

Similar to #36724 .

pulls.title: descriptor, rpc, wallet: do not echo key material in error messages
pulls.body:
Some descriptor error messages quote the string the caller sent, and a descriptor can hold a private key. The error then carries the key, or part of it, into places the request may not go: an application's log, an error reporter, a screenshot shared for help.

This PR stops the quoting. A failing key is named by its position, a failing entry of `solving_data.descriptors` by its index, and a function name is quoted only where the parser accepts it. The commit message lists each changed error.

| before | after |
| --- | --- |
| `key '<key>' is not valid` | `key is not valid` |
| `Multi: key '<key>' is not valid` | `Multi: key 3: key is not valid` |
| `'wpkh(<key>)x' is not a valid descriptor function` | `Unexpected text after the closing ')' of wpkh()` |
| `'<start of a key>(<rest>' is not a valid descriptor function` | `Not a valid descriptor expression` |
| `Unable to parse descriptor '<descriptor>': Missing checksum` | `Unable to parse descriptor at index 1: Missing checksum` |
| `Could not add descriptor '<descriptor>': ...` | the same, quoting the public form of the descriptor |

pulls.body:
The changes can be verified by running `test/lint/git-subtree-check.sh src/ipc/libmultiprocess` as described in [developer notes](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/master/doc/developer-notes.md#subtrees) and [lint instructions](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/tree/master/test/lint#git-subtree-checksh).

Changes since last subtree update (#35720):

- Adds support for nonunix platforms, making API changes that are not backwards compatible ([#274](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess/pull/274)). Follow-ups add a `CurrentThread()` accessor matching compatibility code in [bitcoin/bitcoin#35084](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35084) ([#323](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess/pull/323)) and remove code for Cap'n Proto versions before 0.9 ([#331](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess/pull/331)).
- Fixes a data race between IPC calls running on worker threads and disconnects, found by Antithesis ([#349](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess/pull/349)).
- Fixes a use-after-free when a socket disconnects before `ConnectStream` connects, and leaks and hangs when a client `construct()` call throws ([#298](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess/pull/298)).
- Fixes a race where file descriptors from `SpawnProcess` could leak into processes forked at the same time by other threads, by clearing `FD_CLOEXEC` in the child after forking ([#311](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess/pull/311)).
- Makes `SpawnProcess` report `exec` failures back to the parent and throw, reaping the child ([#312](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess/pull/312)).
- Adds support for `std::chrono::time_point` fields ([#303](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess/pull/303)) and for serializing lists of interface objects that need to be moved from ([#304](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess/pull/304)), both needed by [bitcoin/bitcoin#10102](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/10102).
- Accepts container fields and parameters with any comparator, hash, and allocator types, like Bitcoin Core's `GCSFilter::ElementSet`, needed by [bitcoin/bitcoin#29409](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/29409) ([#379](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess/pull/379)).

pulls.title: wallet: Fix detection of symlinks on Windows
pulls.body:
This PR implements symlink detection for Windows, since GCC [doesn't support symlinks on Windows](https://gcc.gnu.org/git/?p=gcc.git;a=blob;f=libstdc%2B%2B-v3/src/filesystem/ops-common.h;h=ba377905a2e90f7baf30c900b090f1f732397e08;hb=refs/heads/releases/gcc-13#l124). This is used by the wallet's `ListDatabases` in order to detect symlinks and avoid recursing them. It's also used in wallet path validation since that is also checking whether paths are symlinks, and we should properly detect symlinks on Windows.

Under the hood, the `IsSymlink` function uses `std::filesystem::is_symlink` for non-Windows systems. On Windows, it checks a file's attributes to determine if it is a [reparse point](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/fileio/reparse-points). Strictly speaking, this will also catch files that aren't symlinks, such as directories that are Onedrive mounts. I think it's fine to not be recursively searching such directories.

This is based on #34418 for the multiwallet test and CI changes that it enables. The last commit also removes the skipping of the symlink checks so that we are testing that the symlink handling behavior on Windows matches that on Linux and MacOS.

pulls.title: http: Restore requirement of IPv4 bind success
pulls.body:
### Problem

When bitcoind starts and the HTTP IPv4 listen address is occupied by another process, but the IPv6 address is available, the server fails open and generates a cookie file. When bitcoin-cli runs it picks up the cookie file and sends the credentials in plain text to the non-bitcoind process running on the default IPv4 port. An attacker can then use the credentials to commandeer bitcoind over IPv6.

### Solution

*Safe defaults*:
* When running with default settings, require that the IPv4 bind succeeds.
* When `-rpcbind` is specified, require that all HTTP listen socket binds succeed (fail closed-behavior).

Node runners who only have IPv6 are now required to override `-rpcbind` to only specify the working interface if they were not doing so already.

The problem of bitcoin-cli sending the credentials to what could possibly be the wrong process remains **only in non-default setups**.

### History

40b556d3742a1f65d67e2d4c760d0b13fe8be5b7 from 2015 switched the HTTP server from Boost Asio to LibEvent, and binding switched from an attempt at dual-binding IPv4+v6 and falling back to IPv4-only (rpcserver.cpp / `StartRPCThreads()`), to binding IPv4 *or* IPv6 (httpserver.cpp / `HTTPBindAddresses()`). **The current PR restores the prior behavior of IPv4 being mandatory.**

#14968 from 2018 was an attempt to change the behavior to require *all* binds to succeed. But it ran into issues with poor IPv6 support on CI.

### Severity

This credential exfiltration attack requires capability to launch processes on the bitcoind host. If we are on the same account we can already read the cookie credentials off disk. So it's only really interesting when an attacker is on a different user account on the same host.

### Disclaimer

The 2 commits with multiple authors were probably initially generated with the help of silicon LLMs.

pulls.title: wallet: rpc: Deprecate `encryptwallet` RPC for encrypting existing wallets.
pulls.body:
For more context, see: #36027

Encrypting existing wallets that are unencrypted is fraught with footguns and complexity both for users and for developers.

For example:

- No efforts are made to ensure that remnants of unencrypted key material are not left on the user's disk, as attempting to ensure this would be difficult and dangerous, and for some SSD's infeasible.

- Encrypting a wallet that has manually imported descriptors will cause the wallet to change the spending conditions out from under the user. (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/26607)

- Because new keys are made after encryption, restoring from a backup made before encryption may result in loss of funds.

pulls.title: addrman, rpc: classify linked-IPv4 addresses consistently
pulls.body:
Some addresses can be an IPv6 ones with an embedded IPv4 address belongs to. `AddrMan::Size()`, and so the per-network counts in `getaddrmaninfo`, use `GetNetwork()`, which returns ipv6 for these addresses. However, the network filter in `GetAddr_()` and the network / source_network labels in `getnodeaddresses` and `getrawaddrman` use `GetNetClass()`, which returns ipv4 for them.

So on master, for example, for a node whose addrman holds a 6to4 or Teredo address:
  - getaddrmaninfo counts it under ipv6.
  - getnodeaddresses 0 "ipv6" doesn't return it.
  - getnodeaddresses 0 "ipv4" does return it, labelled ipv4.

This PR changes all of this places to use `GetNetwork()`. This way the filter, labels and the counts agree. We should leave `GetNetClass()` usage for netgroup and bucketing decisions, where treating linked-IPv4 addresses as IPv4 is intended. If you pick the change in the fuzz target and run it without the other changes, it's expected to crash to reproduce the issue.

pulls.title: psbt: accept taproot ALL sigs with sighash unset
pulls.body:
SignPSBTInput() assumes SIGHASH_DEFAULT for a taproot input when
neither PSBT_IN_SIGHASH_TYPE nor the caller's sighash_type is set.
Its check of existing signatures then rejected every 65-byte
taproot signature, so a PSBT holding a valid SIGHASH_ALL signature
could be neither finalized nor signed further.

When neither the field nor the parameter is set, the default is only
assumed, so also accept a 65-byte signature ending in SIGHASH_ALL.
NONE, SINGLE and ANYONECANPAY variants are still rejected, as are
all mismatches when the field or the parameter is set.

Fixes #36507.

pulls.title: refactor: Change some validation.cpp methods to return BlockValidationState
pulls.body:
**Summary**. Refactor validation result to be a return value instead of an output parameter in several `validation.cpp` methods.

**Motivation**. The benefits of the change are:
- Exclude the potentially inconsistent case when the bool return value and the returned `state` are inconsistent
- Exclude the ambiguity whether the passed in value of state is used or not (not obvious in chained calls)
- Remove the possibility of unintuitive interaction between subsequent calls with the same state. In case of a validation error, a failure reason is set if the state was valid, but not if it was already invalid.
- Slightly simpler: It's more evident which is the result; one less parameters.

This has grown out from #33856, mentioned in [comment here](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/33856#pullrequestreview-4276791829) and [here](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/33856#issuecomment-4477751949).

**Details**. Many methods follow the scheme where the validation state is returned in an output parameter (`BlockValidationState& state`), and and additional `bool` return value indicating success. In success case the convention is that `state.IsValid()` and the return value are both true. After the change there is only a `BlockValidationState` return value, which is either success (`state.IsValid() == true`), or an invalid/error case.

This change is a highly localized refactor, but touching a sensitive file.

Relevant methods called by `ProcessNewBlockHeaders` and `AcceptBlock` (directly and indirectly) are touched.

Changes are separated into commits by touched methods, ordered by bottom-to-top in the call hierarchy.

This makes `bitcoin-wallet dump` fail if writing the dump file does not complete successfully.

pulls.title: descriptor: speed-up `Parse` (xpub/xpriv) in ~30%
pulls.body:
This PR speeds up descriptor parsing, for basically descriptors that use xpub/xpriv, through some targeted improvements (I've been working on fuzz targets for wallet stuff for a while. I've noticed that some of them are slow so I started to work on understanding why and improve what can be improved. The finding came from it):

- Avoid redundant base58 decoding when parsing extended keys (this is the major improvement)

  ParsePubkeyInner unconditionally called both DecodeExtKey() and DecodeExtPubKey(), each running a full DecodeBase58Check (two SHA256 passes over ~111 bytes). A new DecodeExtKeyOrPubKey() function performs a single base58 decode and then checks the prefix, halving the cryptographic work per key. The interfaces of DecodeSecret, DecodeExtKey, and DecodeExtPubKey are also updated to accept string_view instead of const std::string&, eliminating unnecessary string copies in the descriptor parser and allowing DecodeBase58/DecodeBase58Check to use pointer-range iteration instead of strlen.

- Replace O(n) charset lookup with precomputed table

  DescriptorChecksum previously called std::string::find() for every character in the descriptor string, doing up to 96 comparisons per character. This replaces it with a 256-entry precomputed lookup table for O(1) lookups. The benefit scales with descriptor length.

pulls.title: wallet: Fix ScanForWalletTransactions missing tx when look-ahead pool expands mid-block
pulls.body:
When `ScanForWalletTransactions` processes a block containing both a transaction to a key just outside the look-ahead pool and a pool-expanding transaction that triggers `TopUp`, and the former appears first in vtx order, the wallet misses the earlier transaction — leaving the balance wrong with no indication a second scan is needed. The fix retries any transaction that doesn't match on a full pass, dropping it once it does, until a pass resolves nothing new — so a transaction can be recognized once something else in the block makes it relevant, regardless of why. The first commit demonstrates the incorrect behaviour; the second contains the fix; the third adds a benchmark guarding the fix's performance on a large, mostly-foreign block with an embedded multi-level cascade.
Bug details...
`ScanForWalletTransactions` iterates over a block's transactions in the order the miner placed them (vtx order). A descriptor wallet maintains a look-ahead pool of pre-derived keys so it can recognise incoming payments. When a payment arrives at a key near the pool boundary, `MarkUnusedAddresses` → `TopUp` extends the pool. If within a single block: - **Tx_lookahead** pays to key index `N` (just outside the current pool `[0, N-1]`), AND - **Tx_expand** pays to key index `N-1` (last in pool — triggers TopUp, extending pool to `[0, 2N-1]`) and Tx_lookahead appears at an earlier vtx position than Tx_expand, the scan misses Tx_lookahead: 1. Tx_lookahead processed: pool = `[0, N-1]` → `IsMine` returns false → missed 2. Tx_expand processed: key `N-1` found → TopUp fires → pool = `[0, 2N-1]` `FastWalletRescanFilter::UpdateIfNeeded()` fires only at the **start of the next block** iteration — there is no mechanism to re-examine Tx_lookahead within the same scan pass. The transaction is not permanently lost — because Tx_expand extended the pool as a side effect, a second explicit `rescanblockchain` call recovers Tx_lookahead. But the wallet shows a wrong balance with no indication a second scan is needed. This bug does not affect live `blockConnected` when both transactions pass through the mempool first: `transactionAddedToMempool(Tx_expand)` pre-extends the pool before the block arrives, so vtx ordering does not matter. It only manifests in `ScanForWalletTransactions` (rescan paths) for descriptor wallets.
Affected callers...
**Callers affected** (all use `ScanForWalletTransactions`): - `rescanblockchain` - `importdescriptors` (via `RescanFromTime`) - `restorewallet` and wallet migration watchonly/solvable wallets (via `AttachChain`)
Fix details and performance...
**Fix:** during the per-block vtx loop, keep a list of still-unmatched vtx positions. Retry it each pass, dropping positions once `SyncTransaction()` returns `true` for them, until a full pass resolves nothing new. A transaction becomes resolvable once something else earlier in the same block changes its relevance — either a pool expansion (`TopUp` from `MarkUnusedAddresses`) now covering a key it pays, or a previously-unknown parent transaction becoming known so a spend of it is recognized. The unmatched set never grows, so this terminates without a safety cap. This also covers two cases a shrinking-prefix rescan (an earlier version of this fix) did not: a prefix-recovered receive that triggers a second pool expansion past where the prefix had already shrunk to (see Part 5), and a same-block spend of a look-ahead receive only recognized later in the same pass via a parent-tx lookup rather than a pool expansion (see Part 6, molnard's finding — see Notes below). **Performance:** the retry loop costs at most one extra pass for any block containing a wallet-relevant transaction during a rescan, in typical shapes. The worst case is a large, mostly-foreign block with a multi-level cascade embedded in it. `bench_bitcoin -filter=RescanCascadeInLargeBlock` guards that scenario against regression.
Test coverage...
**Regression test:** `test/functional/wallet_rescan_intrablock_ordering.py` - Part 1: loadwallet rescan — Tx_lookahead found after fix. - Part 2: importdescriptors full rescan from genesis — Tx_lookahead found after fix. - Part 3: second rescanblockchain recovers Tx_lookahead (pre-fix behaviour, kept as sanity check). - Part 4: two-level cascade — two successive TopUp events fire in one block, both lookahead txs found, validating the bounded multi-pass loop. - Part 5: a prefix-recovered receive triggers a second TopUp past where a shrinking-prefix rescan would have already stopped. - Part 6: a same-block spend of a look-ahead receive only recognized later in the same pass (molnard's finding).
Manual reproduction (regtest) ```bash bitcoind -regtest -keypool=5 -fallbackfee=0.0001 -daemon bitcoin-cli -regtest -named createwallet wallet_name=funding bitcoin-cli -regtest generatetoaddress 102 $(bitcoin-cli -regtest -rpcwallet=funding getnewaddress) bitcoin-cli -regtest -named createwallet wallet_name=test RECV_DESC=$(bitcoin-cli -regtest -rpcwallet=test listdescriptors \ | jq -r '[.descriptors[] | select(.internal==false and .range!=null)][0].desc') END_RANGE=$(bitcoin-cli -regtest -rpcwallet=test listdescriptors \ | jq '[.descriptors[] | select(.internal==false and .range!=null)][0].range[1]') ADDR_EXPAND=$(bitcoin-cli -regtest deriveaddresses "$RECV_DESC" "[$END_RANGE,$END_RANGE]" | jq -r '.[0]') ADDR_LOOKAHEAD=$(bitcoin-cli -regtest deriveaddresses "$RECV_DESC" "[$((END_RANGE+1)),$((END_RANGE+1))]" | jq -r '.[0]') bitcoin-cli -regtest unloadwallet test TXID1=$(bitcoin-cli -regtest -rpcwallet=funding sendtoaddress "$ADDR_LOOKAHEAD" 0.001) TXID2=$(bitcoin-cli -regtest -rpcwallet=funding sendtoaddress "$ADDR_EXPAND" 0.001) bitcoin-cli -regtest generateblock "raw(51)" "[\"$TXID1\",\"$TXID2\"]" # First scan — TXID1 missing, wrong balance bitcoin-cli -regtest loadwallet test bitcoin-cli -regtest -rpcwallet=test listtransactions # Second scan — TXID1 recovered bitcoin-cli -regtest -rpcwallet=test rescanblockchain bitcoin-cli -regtest -rpcwallet=test listtransactions # With the fix (this PR's tip), both transactions are found on the first scan. bitcoin-cli -regtest loadwallet test bitcoin-cli -regtest -rpcwallet=test listtransactions ```
_**Notes**_: * Originally noted by furszy in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/31629#issuecomment-2657775368; his "case 2" describes a related but harder inter-block variant: new blocks arriving via `blockConnected` during an active rescan with a not-yet-expanded pool. That problem remains a potential follow-up. This PR fixes the simpler intra-block sub-case where the miss happens entirely within a single block's vtx loop, with no concurrent block arrivals required. * Perhaps the issue is related to the symptom was previously reported in #19808 but could not be reproduced at the time and was closed without a fix. * molnard [found](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35901#pullrequestreview-5041935034) a related gap the shrinking-prefix rescan didn't close: if a parent tx pays a look-ahead key and a later tx in the same block spends that parent's output, and the spend sits at or after the block's last pool expansion, the prefix rescan recovers the parent but never revisits the spend. jeanpablojp separately found a second gap in the same shrinking-prefix approach — a prefix-recovered receive that triggers a further pool expansion past where the prefix had already shrunk to (Part 5) — and proposed and benchmarked the fix now in this PR: retry based on each tx's `SyncTransaction()` result until a full pass causes no change, rather than tracking a shrinking prefix. Both gaps are now fixed in this PR (Parts 5 and 6).

pulls.title: private broadcast: Extra guard against unintended non-private broadcast of private transactions
pulls.body:
Motivation: Reduce the risk of accidental privacy leak happening when broadcasting non-privately a requested transaction that had been previously broadcast privately.

Background: During the initial phase of private broadcast implementation there were unforeseen instances when a private transaction could get broadcast non-privately (see #35032 #35319 #35410 #36309 #36312 #36277 #36330).

Currently known pathways:

- Re-submission through `submitpackage`
- Wallet-rebroadcast (when a private transaction is "picked up" by the wallet, and rebrodcast after 1-2 days)

Note that these are being addressed, but other, currently non-identified pathways cannot be excluded.

Change summary: Add a general, extra safeguard: whenever there is a transaction broadcast request, check if the given transaction has been previously broadcast privately, and if so, refuse to broadcast non-privately.

Transaction relay is not affected, as it should not be affected by private broadcast.  When we receive a previously private-broadcast transaction for the first time (it's not yet in our mempool), we relay it as any other relayed transaction. Behavior is unchanged in this regard.

Notes:

- Prerequisite: This is built on top of #36477, as keeping finished private broadcasts in the queue is a prerequisite for this change to work.
- This proposed change is not an alternative to the use-case specific safeguards, but a complementary one.
- Testing currently uses the two pathways listed above. When they are closed, testing will be more difficult (i.e., it is hard to establish whether non-private broadcast is prevented by the use-case specific or the present generic guard).
- The private broadcast queue is not persisted, it doesn't survive node restarts
- Entries deleted via `abortprivatebroadcast` will be forgotten.

Keeping as Draft, because the prerequisite #36477 is pending.

pulls.title: node: batch block file pruning in a single pass over block index
pulls.body:
When starting a node with pruning enabled (e.g. `-prune=550`) on a node with full chain history or pruning many files at once, `FindFilesToPrune` and `FindFilesToPruneManual` previously called `PruneOneBlockFile` once per file.

Because `PruneOneBlockFile` iterated over the entire `m_block_index` for each file, this was an O(M * N) operation (M = files to prune, N = total blocks). When pruning a full chain (~5,770 files and ~972k blocks), this triggered ~5.6 billion iterations and froze the node running on a Pi 5 for ~10 minutes on startup while holding `cs_main`.

This PR replaces `PruneOneBlockFile` with `PruneBlockFiles(const std::set<int>&)`, which collects all candidate files and prunes them in a single O(M + N) pass over `m_block_index` using a compact dynamic bitfield (`std::vector<bool>`). Also skips entries without block or undo data to avoid unneeded checks and prevent file 0 pruning from dirtying header-only or already-pruned index entries. The new signature is analogous to `UnlinkPrunedFiles({file_number});`.

Benchmarked with ~972k blocks and 5,770 files to prune:
- x86_64 (i7-8665U @ 1.90 GHz): 75.1s -> 14.7ms (~5,100x speedup)
- ARM64 (Raspberry Pi 5): 606.0s -> 26.3ms (>3,500x speedup)

Both timings were taken with a datadir whose block index and block file info records came from a full chain, with the `blk*.dat` and `rev*.dat` files backfilled as 0-byte files. Pruning selection reads only the index and the file info, so empty files reproduce the startup cost without a full chain, and `UnlinkPrunedFiles` deletes them cheaply.

A case where this matters in practice is a pruned node restarting after a long outage. It downloads headers for the whole gap first, leaving many header-only entries behind, then has to prune a large backlog in a few flushes. The data-less skip avoids re-dirtying all of those entries, and the single pass bounds the work by the index size instead of files times index size.

Add unit test `blockmanager_prune_block_files_batch` to verify batch pruning, empty set no-ops, clean dirty-set behavior, and cleared block and undo metadata. Add a test for the `FindFilesToPruneManual` caller path, including a mixed valid and out-of-range file set. Update caller tests in `blockmanager_tests` and `rescan_tests`.

pulls.title: Wallet: Don't backdate locktime rbf
pulls.body:
Closes https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/26526 Currently, in Bitcoin Core, given an original transaction A and its replacement B, we refer to **backdating** when the locktime of A is higher than the locktime of B (`A.locktime > B.locktime`). This can happen because Bitcoin Core enables **anti-fee-sniping** by default, which sets the transaction's locktime to the current block height. For privacy, 10% of the time, it instead sets a different locktime, randomly chosen between the current height and the current height minus 100 blocks. This can lead into having a replacement of a transaction with a locktime older than its original transaction. This is unrealistics and can be used as a wallet fingerprint. You can find a functional test to reproduce the behaviour mentioned [here](https://gist.github.com/Bicaru20/9afcb878dd103369255cd81cffac86ba) The approach proposed in this PR adds a new parameter to `CoinControl` to keep track of the previous locktime in the case of a `bumpfee`. We then pass this parameter to the DiscourageFeeSniping function through a new parameter, `minimum_height`, whose default value is set to 0.
Alternative approach: Since the locktime of the new transaction is 0, we also considered setting it to the previous locktime value and then, inside `DiscourageFeeSniping`, saving the previous locktime and setting the transaction's locktime to the block height before applying any of the backdating logic. This way, we could avoid passing a new parameter to the function. We ultimately decided not to go with this approach, as it makes the code more difficult to follow.
The only RPC that is affected by this changes is `bumpfee`. The pr also includes a functional test in `wallet_bumpfee.py` to test that when replacing a transation using `bumpfee` the locktime is not backdated.
We also conducted a small analysis to see how many the backdating in RBF transactions actually happen. We have data on the replaced transactions from 2025-05-01 to 2026-06-01. With that we have been able to detect this many backdatings: _We took the date of the last transaction of the replacement chain (A replacement chain are all the transactions that replace themselves)_ In total we have over 1,000,000 rbf transactions, but we see that on average there are only about 200-300 hundred replaccements backdating per week. Looking at the percentages we see that on average is less than 2% of all the transactions that have been replaced. So, it is clear that backdating in replacement transactions is unusual. However, the few transactions that do exhibit backdating are easily fingerprintable as having been replaced using `bumpfee` in Bitcoin Core or Electrum.

pulls.body:
**Problem:** The oversized-script fallback appends `OP_RETURN` to the destination instead of replacing it. If the destination already contains an unfinished push, the appended byte becomes pushed data and the result can remain spendable.

pulls.title: CAT in Tapscript (BIP-347)
pulls.body:
# CAT in Tapscript

This PR provides the necessary code to enable the opcode OP\_CAT in Tapscript as specified in [BIP-347: OP\_CAT in Tapscript](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0347.mediawiki) and [BIN-2024-0001](https://github.com/bitcoin-inquisition/binana/blob/master/2024/BIN-2024-0001.md),

**Important:** This PR *does not* include miner activation functionality. This means that merging this PR into bitcoin-core will not make OP\_CAT functional in Bitcoin.
If this PR is merged it is *not* a signal of community consensus around activating CAT nor be read as a portent about the activation process or timeline.
The PR is not a stand-in for consensus around such decisions.

This PR includes:

- An implementation of the Tapscript opcode OP\_CAT along with the flags `SCRIPT_VERIFY_OP_CAT` and `SCRIPT_VERIFY_DISCOURAGE_OP_CAT`.
- Integration and unit tests which ensure that our CAT  implementation works as expected. This includes ensuring that CAT never uses more that 520 bytes of stack memory. A full description of what these tests cover is given below.
- An improvement to `src/test/script_tests.cpp` JSON script format enabling the rapid creation of new Tapscript unit tests.

## Activation on Bitcoin-inquisition (signet)

[Bitcoin-inquisition PR 37](https://github.com/bitcoin-inquisition/bitcoin/pull/39) which contained our implementation of OP\_CAT [was merged into bitcoin-inquisition (signet) on Apr 25 2024](https://github.com/bitcoin-inquisition/bitcoin/pull/39), released as [bitcoin-inquisition release 25.2 on Apr 26 2024.](https://github.com/bitcoin-inquisition/bitcoin/releases/tag/v25.2-inq) and activated in bitcoin-inquisition Apr 30 2024. The bitcoin-inquisition PR was reviewed in the PR review club [(transcript of discussion)](https://bitcoincore.reviews/bitcoin-inquisition-39). Since Apr 30 2024 there have been many OP\_CAT transactions created and spent on signet.

The code merged into bitcoin-inquisition differs from this PR, as we have removed the consensus logic which was used to activate it on signet.

## OP\_CAT Tapscript Implementation

We implement OP\_CAT as a new Tapscript op code by redefining the opcode OP\_SUCCESS126 (126 in decimal and 0x7e in hexadecimal). This is the same opcode value used by the original OP_CAT.

When evaluated, the OP\_CAT instruction:

1. Pops the top two values off the stack,
2. concatenates the popped values together in stack order,
3. and then pushes the concatenated value on the top of the stack.

OP\_CAT fails if there are fewer than two values on the stack or if a concatenated value would have a combined size greater than the maximum script element size of 520 bytes.

See [BIP 347](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0347.mediawiki) for a deeper description.

### Errors thrown

If evaluated OP\_CAT can throw the following errors:

- If at time of evaluation the stack has fewer than two elements we throw the error: `SCRIPT_ERR_INVALID_STACK_OPERATION`
- If at time of evaluation the top two stack elements have a combined size greater than `MAX_SCRIPT_ELEMENT_SIZE` (520 bytes) we throw the error: `SCRIPT_ERR_PUSH_SIZE`.

### Script verification flags

While this PR does not contain any miner signaling and activation logic and can not activate OP\_CAT, it does contain two flags which future activation logic could set to control activation of OP\_CAT.

- `SCRIPT_VERIFY_OP_CAT` IF a bitcoin node has this set to true, then it treat OP\_CAT enabled for Tapscript. That is, OP\_SUCCESS126 will be redefining to OP\_CAT in Tapscript. If this was set to true at the consensus level this would cause a soft fork.

`SCRIPT_VERIFY_DISCOURAGE_OP_CAT` When set to true, a node receiving any Tapscript transaction containing the opcode OP\_CAT or OP\_SUCCESS126 will reject the transaction throwing the error `SCRIPT_ERR_DISCOURAGE_OP_CAT` but not banning the node which relayed the transaction. This prevents nodes from relaying transactions with OP\_CAT. This  is equivalent to the behavior of `SCRIPT_ERR_DISCOURAGE_OP_CAT = true` when `SCRIPT_VERIFY_OP_CAT = false` as OP\_CAT is an OP\_SUCCESS (OP\_SUCCESS126).

This is how these two flags are intended to be used to ensure a smooth soft fork.

| Stage | `SCRIPT_VERIFY OP_CAT` | `SCRIPT_VERIFY DISCOURAGE_OP_CAT` | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **1.Default** | False | True | This does not represent any change in behavior of the bitcoin-core node. |
| **2.Upgrading** | True | True | OP\_CAT is activating. |
| **3.Upgraded** | True | False | It is clear that OP\_CAT has been activated and the network has been upgraded. |

The flag `SCRIPT_ERR_DISCOURAGE_OP_CAT` provides a window of time for the network to fully activate, before nodes will relay or accept transactions containing OP\_CAT in their mem pools.

## Tests

This PR contains a suite of script tests to ensure that OP\_CAT functions as expected. In the JSON script tests (`script_tests.json`), we test:

- That if OP\_CAT is not activated that there are no changes to bitcoin consensus.
- That regardless of the activation or non-activation of OP\_CAT in Tapscript, pre-Tapscript scripts, i.e. Bitcoin scripts, have no changes in behavior.
- That OP\_CAT when evaluated throws the expected error when there are less than two elements on the stack.
- That OP\_CAT when evaluated in a variety of circumstances and edge cases, successfully concatenates elements of the stack. This includes:
  - multiple calls to OP\_CAT in a row,
  - evaluating OP\_CAT inside of a IF conditional,
  - evaluating OP\_CAT on zero size stack elements, random and large stack elements,
  - evaluating OP\_CAT on values being moved to and from the alt stack,
  - and checking that when evaluated OP\_CAT concatenates the elements in the expected order.

All of these tests are designed to cover the happy path of OP\_CAT, the various errors which OP\_CAT can throw and all the corner cases between those two outcomes.

Additionally we include three tests outside of the JSON script tests.

- `cat_simple` and `cat_empty_stack` are designed to test OP\_CAT outside of the JSON serialization regime. Ensure that we catch bugs that we might miss in the JSON script tests due to a bug introduced at the JSON serialization layer.
- `cat_dup_test` enumerates all stack element sizes from 1 to 522 bytes and then enumerates up to 10 repetitions of `OP\_DUP OP\_CAT`. It then tests if the stack element would exceed 520 bytes and if so did OP\_CAT throw the error `SCRIPT_ERR_PUSH_SIZE`. This allows us to be certain that OP\_CAT will not introduce any `OP\_DUP OP\_CAT` memory exhaustion attacks.

### Better Tapscript tests in JSON script tests

While writing these JSON script tests (`script_tests.json`) we ran into the following problem. The JSON script tests are simple and easy to write for pre-Tapscript scripts, but adding or changing a Tapscript test requires substantial work per test.
Consider the following pre-tapscript test:

```json
["'aa' 'bb'", "CAT 0x4c 0x02 0xaabb EQUAL", "P2SH,STRICTENC", "DISABLED_OPCODE", "CAT disabled"]
```

whereas a Tapscript test for the same script (annotated with comments for better readability) would look like:

```json
[
    [
        "aa",
        "bb",
        "7e4c02aabb87", // output script
        "c0d6889cb081036e0faefa3a35157ad71086b123b2b144b649798b494c300a961d", // control block
        0.00000001
    ],
    "",
    "0x51 0x20 0x15048ed3a65748549c27b671936987093cf73a4c9cb18522a74fb9553060ca99", // Tapscript output
    "P2SH,WITNESS,TAPROOT",
    "OK",
    "TAPSCRIPT CATs aa and bb together and checks if EQUAL to aabb"
]
```

Computing the Tapscript output, such as `0x51 0x20 0x15048ed3a65748549c27b671936987093cf73a4c9cb18522a74fb9553060ca99`, requires writing custom code and running it for each test. The same is true for the Tapscript control block, such as `c0d6889cb081036e0faefa3a35157ad71086b123b2b144b649798b494c300a961d`. If a test is changed or updated new outputs and control blocks must be computed. The complexity of doing this is likely the reason that no one has added any Tapscript tests to JSON script tests until this PR.

In this PR we address this issue by adding the following improvements to JSON script tests:

- Adding simple macros (`"#SCRIPT#` and `#CONTROLBLOCK#`) that allow the script test parser to automatically generate and inject a valid Tapscript output and control block to be computed automatically from the JSON script.
- Allowing Tapscript scripts to use the human readable strings like pre-script scripts by marking the location of the script in the witness stack using `#SCRIPT#`. This transforms the unreadable script `7e4c02aabb87` into `#SCRIPT# CAT 0x4c 0x02 0xaabb EQUAL`.

This results in the following JSON script test which is far easier to write and easier to read.

```json
[
    [
        "aa",
        "bb",
        "#SCRIPT# CAT",
        "#CONTROLBLOCK#",
        0.00000001
    ],
    "",
    "0x51 0x20 #TAPROOTOUTPUT#",
    "P2SH,WITNESS,TAPROOT,OP_CAT",
    "OK",
    "TAPSCRIPT Test of OP_CAT flag by calling CAT on two elements. TAPSCRIPT_OP_CAT flag is set so CAT is executed."
],
```

pulls.title: net_processing: count presync work in chain sync eviction
pulls.body:
While our best header is below `-minimumchainwork`, a peer's headers first go through the PRESYNC phase of `HeadersSyncState`, and none of them are stored. So `pindexBestKnownBlock` stays null for the peer we're syncing from, and `ConsiderEviction` (net_processing.cpp:5504) treats it like an outbound peer that never announced a block:

1. it starts `CHAIN_SYNC_TIMEOUT` (20 min)
2. it sends a getheaders to "verify chain work"
3. after `HEADERS_RESPONSE_TIME` it disconnects with `Outbound peer has old chain, best known block = <none>`

This happens even though the peer is still sending headers. The presync progress is lost and the next peer starts from scratch.

On mainnet presync is roughly 480 headers round trips. If that takes more than ~22 minutes (about 2.5 s per round trip, e.g. over slow Tor or I2P), the sync peer gets evicted before presync can finish, and the same thing can happen with the next peer. The chain sync logic is from #11490, presync came later in #25717, and the two were never connected.

The timeout is not reset on presync work alone. When it is set, the work the peer has shown during presync is recorded, and when it expires the timeout is renewed for another `CHAIN_SYNC_TIMEOUT` only if that work has increased since. A peer that stops sending headers is therefore still asked once with getheaders and then disconnected, within about two periods (~42 minutes), as before. `m_headers_sync_mutex` is never held while taking `cs_main`, and `p2p_headers_sync_with_minchainwork.py` and `p2p_sendheaders.py` also pass with `DEBUG_LOCKORDER`.

The new `test_presync_peer_not_evicted` in `p2p_headers_sync_with_minchainwork.py` restarts a node with `-minimumchainwork=0x20000` (65536 headers). An outbound peer then sends it one full headers message per mocked minute for 25 minutes, so presync is still running at the end. On master the peer is disconnected after 24 minutes. With the fix it stays connected and `presynced_headers` keeps going up. `p2p_outbound_eviction.py`, `p2p_eviction.py` and `feature_minchainwork.py` still pass.

`test_presync_peer_stalled_is_evicted` covers the other side: a single outbound peer sends one headers message and then only answers pings, and it is disconnected after about 42 minutes of mocktime. That test fails without the progress check.
